paragraphs: This position paper argues that AI safety should include the ability to improve through repeated encounters with unusual situations. The authors call this an antifragile perspective: a system’s capacity to handle rare or unfamiliar events should adapt and expand with experience. The aim is continuing preparation for changing conditions, including uncertainties greater than those currently understood.

The paper examines why static benchmarks and one-time robustness tests can miss this requirement. Environments evolve, while systems that are insufficiently challenged can become poorly adapted. The authors identify concerns including limited scenario diversity, reward hacking, excessive optimization, and the weakening of broader capabilities. Passing a fixed evaluation therefore does not capture the full process of maintaining safety over time.

The proposed direction is to reconsider how safety is measured, tested, and continually improved. The authors explore dynamic approaches and offer ethical and practical guidance for research. These proposals complement existing robustness work; they present a case for studying long-term adaptation, rather than report a demonstrated solution to rare-event safety.
icml-2025-position-ai-safety-must-embrac.tldr: The authors argue that AI safety should assess how systems improve through repeated exposure to rare and changing situations.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that the future of work belongs within AI safety. The authors recognize concerns about harmful content, manipulation, and catastrophic misuse, but contend that these priorities leave important questions about livelihoods and human agency underexamined. They advocate transition support that helps meaningful work evolve as AI changes the economy.

Using economic theories, the paper considers how AI’s effects on livelihoods unfold over time and how changes in labor markets can worsen income inequality. It also criticizes the closed-source practices of major AI stakeholders as resembling rent seeking. In the authors’ account, these practices can exploit resources, weaken creative labor, and concentrate control over innovation.

The recommendations connect worker protection with the treatment of training data. The authors favor an international copyright framework and collective licensing to support fair compensation for data use. They also call for global AI governance oriented toward workers, shared prosperity, and economic justice. These are policy positions about how AI development should be governed, rather than evidence that a particular transition program has succeeded.
icml-2025-position-ai-safety-should-prio.tldr: The paper argues that AI safety should prioritize meaningful work, worker agency, and fair compensation for training-data use.

paragraphs: This position paper proposes evaluating people and AI working together on tasks. The authors call these centaur evaluations. Their starting point is that benchmarks help determine what machine learning researchers build, yet current evaluations commonly measure systems operating without humans. That setup leaves the quality of human–AI collaboration outside the central object of evaluation.

Joint evaluations would make human augmentation a more explicit research objective. They would also allow researchers to assess qualities such as helpfulness and interpretability through the interaction between a person and a system. The relevant question becomes how well the combined effort works, including whether the AI’s behavior supports the person participating in the task.

The authors argue that these evaluations can be both more realistic and more demanding than existing approaches. They recommend increasing their use because evaluation choices can steer development toward more effective collaboration. This is a methodological proposal: the abstract presents reasons to measure joint performance, without claiming that every human–AI team will outperform a system or person working alone.
icml-2025-position-ai-should-not-be-an-i.tldr: Centaur evaluations assess humans and AI solving tasks together to direct research toward effective human augmentation.

paragraphs: This position paper proposes studying the collections of functions that machine learning models can represent using algebraic geometry. The focus is on the structure of an entire function space, rather than only an individual trained model. The authors name this research direction neuroalgebraic geometry and present it as a bridge between mathematical geometry and deep learning.

Their main setting is algebraic models, including neural networks whose activation functions are polynomials. The associated function spaces form mathematical objects called semi-algebraic varieties. The paper outlines a dictionary connecting geometric properties, including dimension, degree, and singularities, with machine learning questions about representational power, data requirements, training behavior, and implicit bias.

This perspective matters because it organizes several learning questions around properties of the same underlying function space. The authors review existing literature and also discuss ideas extending beyond the algebraic setting. The contribution is a foundation and research agenda for developing these connections, with algebraic models providing the central setting in which the proposed geometric language applies.
icml-2025-position-algebra-unveils-deep-.tldr: The paper proposes algebraic geometry as a framework for connecting neural-network function spaces with fundamental learning behavior.

paragraphs: This position paper examines who should control language model agents as they increasingly mediate online activity. The authors warn that agents controlled by dominant internet companies, or firms seeking to replace them, will likely reinforce surveillance, dependence on particular platforms, and incumbent power. Their concern is how ownership shapes the choices available to users.

The alternative they propose is an agent advocate: an agent controlled by its user and intended to protect that person’s autonomy and freedom of choice. Making such agents possible requires more than a particular interface or model. The paper treats access to technology, compatibility between systems, and market conditions as connected parts of the same problem.

The authors recommend three coordinated changes: public access to computing resources and capable models outside platform ownership, open standards for interoperability and safety, and regulation preventing platforms from blocking competition. Together, these proposals aim to give user-controlled agents a viable place in the online ecosystem. The predicted harms remain a warning about a likely trajectory, while agent advocates are the authors’ proposed institutional and technical response.
icml-2025-position-build-agent-advocates.tldr: The authors advocate user-controlled AI agents supported by public access, open standards, and competition protections.

paragraphs: This position paper challenges the emphasis on improving language models by increasing their size and the amount of training data. The authors acknowledge that scaling laws have helped explain performance gains. Their concern is that organizing development around continued growth also brings substantial computing costs, environmental consequences, and constraints on where models can be deployed.

The proposed alternative is a broad framework for downscaling. Its goal is to preserve model performance while sharply lowering resource requirements. That framing makes resource use part of the central development objective: progress would include making useful capabilities less demanding to train or deploy, alongside attention to the quality of the model’s outputs.

The paper outlines practical strategies for moving toward this objective and argues that efficiency, sustainability, and accessibility should guide language-model development. The key contribution is a change in research priorities and an organizing framework for pursuing it. Maintaining performance while greatly reducing resource demands is the framework’s stated ambition, rather than a result the abstract establishes for a particular model.
icml-2025-position-enough-of-scaling-llm.tldr: The paper advocates downscaling language models to preserve useful performance while substantially reducing resource demands.

paragraphs: This position paper takes stock of AI for software engineering as an area with substantial progress and substantial unfinished work. The authors describe it as a prominent success of generative AI, while emphasizing that fully automated software engineering remains difficult. They frame further progress as a research challenge shared by academic and industrial communities.

The paper first supplies a taxonomy of tasks and measures. This provides an organizing structure for categorizing research according to the work being addressed and how progress is assessed. The authors then identify bottlenecks that run through current approaches, placing these obstacles within a broader account of what the field still needs to accomplish.

Finally, the paper highlights promising research directions aimed at those bottlenecks. Its contribution is therefore a map linking categories of work, persistent obstacles, and possible routes forward. The distinction between demonstrated progress and full automation is central: success within AI-assisted software engineering does not, in the authors’ assessment, mean the larger goal has already been reached.
icml-2025-position-future-research-and-c.tldr: The paper organizes AI software-engineering research around tasks, evaluation measures, bottlenecks, and directions toward fuller automation.

paragraphs: This position paper distinguishes useful AI capabilities from reasoning that transfers robustly to unfamiliar situations. The authors test language models on algorithmic tasks in esoteric programming languages and report that their reasoning overfits training data and transfers poorly. They hypothesize that this weakness arises partly because learned knowledge and reasoning are coupled within current language models.

They propose separating these roles through three research directions. First, reasoning would be pretrained from scratch using reinforcement learning instead of next-token prediction. Second, a curriculum of synthetic tasks would develop a foundation for reasoning that could transfer to natural-language tasks. Third, a small context window would discourage reliance on misleading correlations between tokens.

The proposed reasoning system would work with a trained retrieval component and a large external memory containing knowledge. The intended benefit is more generalizable reasoning in novel situations without requiring the same component to store all relevant information. The experiments support the concern about transfer; the explanation involving coupled knowledge and reasoning remains a hypothesis motivating the proposed architecture and training agenda.
icml-2025-position-general-intelligence-.tldr: The authors propose reward-based reasoning pretraining and external knowledge storage to address language models’ limited transfer to novel tasks.

paragraphs: This paper develops gradual disempowerment as a possible route to existential risk from AI. It examines how incremental capability improvements could erode human influence over the economy, culture, and government. The concern is a cumulative process in the systems society depends on, without requiring a sudden takeover to explain the loss of control.

The proposed mechanism involves replacing human labor and cognition. This can weaken direct channels of influence, such as voting and consumer choice, as well as indirect incentives to respect human preferences that arise when institutions depend on human participation. More powerful optimization by AI may also amplify mismatches that already exist between institutional behavior and what people want.

The authors argue that changes across these domains could reinforce one another: economic power affects politics and culture, while cultural changes reshape economic and political behavior. They warn that this process could eventually make lost human influence effectively irreversible. Their recommendation is to develop technical research and governance approaches specifically addressing this interconnected erosion of agency; the catastrophic outcome is presented as a risk, not an inevitable forecast.
icml-2025-position-humanity-faces-existe.tldr: Incremental AI advances could create existential risk by progressively and irreversibly weakening human influence over interconnected societal systems.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that general-purpose AI needs stronger arrangements for independent evaluation and flaw reporting. Drawing on collaboration across software security, machine learning, law, social science, and policy, the authors identify gaps in current practices. They describe AI’s reporting infrastructure and norms as substantially less developed than those in software security.

The paper proposes three interventions. Standardized flaw reports and clear rules for researchers would make problems easier to submit, reproduce, and prioritize. Broad disclosure programs inspired by bug bounties would encourage external investigation, with legal protections for researchers. Better coordination infrastructure would distribute relevant reports among the different stakeholders affected by a flaw.

These proposals matter because a vulnerability may extend beyond a single provider’s system. The authors point to jailbreaks and other transferable flaws as evidence that coordinated reporting is urgent. Their contribution is a framework for making external findings actionable across the AI ecosystem. They argue that adopting it could improve safety, security, and accountability, rather than claim that the proposed arrangements have already delivered those improvements.
icml-2025-position-in-house-evaluation-i.tldr: The paper calls for standardized AI flaw reports, protected disclosure programs, and coordinated reporting across affected stakeholders.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that biological neural networks grown in laboratory settings offer a timely opportunity to test ideas about neural computation. Advances in bioengineering have reduced the cost, complexity, and ethical hurdles of working with these systems. The authors see this as a way to bring computational theories into closer contact with living neural activity.

The proposed research direction involves artificial neural networks that interact with and control living neural systems. Such interaction could allow computational models to be evaluated beyond simulation. The paper surveys relevant technologies, principles, and challenges, and describes strategies through which machine learning researchers could investigate this emerging experimental setting.

The longer-term motivation is to learn principles that may help build more robust and energy-efficient AI. The authors also discuss fundamental questions that increasingly sophisticated laboratory neural networks could help answer. These benefits are presented as opportunities enabled by technological progress. The paper’s central contribution is a research case and overview, rather than a claim that biological experimentation has already produced the proposed next generation of AI systems.
icml-2025-position-it-is-time-we-test-ne.tldr: Laboratory-grown neural networks could help test computational theories and inform more robust, energy-efficient AI.

paragraphs: This paper challenges a mismatch between continual reinforcement learning and its evaluation practices. Continual learning aims for agents that keep learning indefinitely, but researchers often choose settings using access to the deployment environment for an entire evaluated lifetime. The authors call this lifetime tuning and argue that it undermines assessment of ongoing learning ability.

They provide empirical evidence using DQN and SAC in continuing and changing environments. Under lifetime tuning, the tested algorithms succeed equally, making it difficult to identify which approaches are better suited to continual learning. When tuning is restricted to only part of an agent’s lifetime, recently developed continual-learning algorithms outperform standard approaches in the reported experiments.

The finding concerns what the evaluation procedure makes visible. Extensive tuning across the full lifetime can conceal differences that emerge when designers have less advance access to the conditions an agent will encounter. The authors use this result to help explain mixed progress in continual reinforcement learning and to motivate empirical practices that better reflect the goal of sustained adaptation.
icml-2025-position-lifetime-tuning-is-in.tldr: The experiments suggest that full-lifetime tuning hides advantages of continual reinforcement-learning methods that appear under limited tuning.

paragraphs: This position paper examines the risks that accompany downloading and reusing openly available machine learning models. Such access lets people use powerful models without the expertise or computing resources needed to develop them. The authors argue that the same ecosystem also contains significant supply-chain risks, some of which have already appeared in real attacks.

The risks span both distribution and development. An attacker could substitute malicious material for a model, while a model’s creation could involve a vulnerable software framework, restricted data, or poisoned data. This framing directs attention to how a model was produced and delivered, alongside the capabilities that make it useful to downstream users.

The paper explores adapting Sigstore, a transparency solution from open-source software, to machine learning models. The proposed use would let publishers sign models and establish properties of the datasets used to create them. The contribution is an argument for stronger transparency around model provenance and inputs. These mechanisms address questions about origin and production history; the abstract does not present them as eliminating every model-related risk.
icml-2025-position-machine-learning-mode.tldr: Open model ecosystems face supply-chain risks, and the paper explores Sigstore for model signing and dataset transparency.

paragraphs: This position paper asks what makes research on surprising deep-learning behavior valuable. It considers phenomena such as double descent, grokking, and the lottery ticket hypothesis. The authors argue that researchers often construct a separate explanation for each phenomenon, even when there is little evidence that the phenomenon appears in real-world applications.

Their concern is about the broader payoff of these explanations. A hypothesis tailored to one isolated observation may contribute less to general understanding than a theory that explains shared principles. The authors therefore recommend treating unusual phenomena as settings for developing and refining broader explanations of deep learning, rather than assuming every puzzle needs its own bespoke resolution.

The paper supports its position by analyzing research outcomes from prominent examples in the literature and offers recommendations for future work. It preserves a constructive role for studying unusual behavior: such cases can help sharpen theories with wider relevance. The proposed standard of value is how well an explanation advances understanding and progress across the field, not merely whether it accounts for one striking observation.
icml-2025-position-not-all-explanations-.tldr: Surprising deep-learning phenomena are most useful when they help refine broad theories rather than only receive isolated explanations.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that complete political neutrality in AI is neither achievable nor always desirable. Judgments about neutrality are subjective, and biases enter through training data, algorithms, and interactions with users. At the same time, the authors maintain that pursuing some degree of neutrality matters because AI can influence people’s opinions and decisions.

Their proposal is to replace an absolute goal of eliminating bias with practical approximations. They introduce eight techniques across three ways of conceptualizing AI and discuss implementation choices and trade-offs. This approach treats neutrality as something that can be pursued to varying degrees, while keeping balanced interaction and reduced manipulation as central motivations.

The paper also examines two concrete applications and demonstrates evaluation of the framework through outputs from current language models. That assessment shows how the proposed approximations can be evaluated; it does not establish that full neutrality has been reached. The contribution is a framework for making a contested ideal more actionable while preserving attention to the choices and compromises involved.
icml-2025-position-political-neutrality-.tldr: The paper proposes practical, evaluable approximations of political neutrality while arguing that complete neutrality is unattainable.

paragraphs: This position paper questions the usual explanation for why spectral graph neural networks work. Their theory centers on a graph Fourier basis formed from eigenvectors of the normalized graph Laplacian, while practical implementations use polynomial approximations. The authors suggest that successful behavior may come from mechanisms that this conventional theoretical account does not adequately capture.

They identify two connected concerns. First, the graph basis may not preserve the meanings associated with Fourier analysis well enough to justify its intended role. Second, barriers to more expressive filters may help protect stability and generalization, rather than merely represent implementation difficulties. Avoiding complex filters has, in their account, also obscured questions about the basis itself.

The resulting position is that these networks may depend less on their Fourier interpretation than commonly assumed. The paper suggests exploring alternative graph dictionaries with clearer semantic meaning and reconsidering what polynomial techniques contribute theoretically. This is a qualified challenge to the explanation of existing success, motivating research into which mathematical structures actually account for the models’ effectiveness.
icml-2025-position-spectral-gnns-rely-le.tldr: Spectral graph neural networks may owe less of their effectiveness to the graph Fourier basis than their standard theory suggests.

paragraphs: This position paper examines methods that detect unfamiliar inputs using the uncertainty or internal features of supervised classifiers. The authors argue that classifying known categories and identifying out-of-distribution inputs are fundamentally misaligned objectives. A classifier trained only to distinguish cats from dogs, for example, can confidently assign an airplane to one of those categories.

The paper identifies a different mistaken equivalence in each major approach. Uncertainty-based methods treat uncertainty as evidence that an input is outside the distribution. Feature-based methods treat distance in the learned representation as evidence of the same thing. The authors show how these mismatches produce irreducible detection errors and identify common settings where the methods are ineffective.

They further argue that combining features and classifier outputs, increasing scale, representing epistemic uncertainty, or exposing models to outliers does not resolve the underlying objective mismatch. The implication concerns the basis for detection: signals learned to separate known classes cannot simply be assumed to answer whether an input belongs to the expected distribution. The paper challenges that assumption rather than offering a simple adjustment.
icml-2025-position-supervised-classifier.tldr: The paper argues that classifier uncertainty and feature distance are fundamentally misaligned with detecting out-of-distribution inputs.

paragraphs: This position paper addresses pressure on AI conference peer review as submission volumes grow and concerns about review quality increase. The authors view the process as an interaction among authors, reviewers, and conferences, with responsibility shared across all three. Their proposed reform concentrates on making reviewers more accountable while recognizing and rewarding high-quality reviewing.

The first mechanism is a two-stage process in which authors can evaluate the reviews they receive. The intention is to create feedback in both directions while minimizing retaliation. The second mechanism is a systematic reward structure, including formal accreditation, that gives reviewers a reason to invest in useful, responsible assessments of submitted work.

These mechanisms connect information about review quality with incentives for improving it. The authors situate this focus alongside their view that author misconduct requires enforcement and detection, while ethical concerns also require self-reflection. The paper calls for community engagement with the reforms as a route toward sustainable peer review; it presents the design and its rationale rather than reporting a demonstrated conference-wide improvement.
icml-2025-position-the-ai-conference-pee.tldr: The authors propose author feedback on reviews and formal reviewer rewards to strengthen accountability in AI conference peer review.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that the human labor embodied in language-model training data deserves a central place in discussions of model cost. Computing, hardware, energy, and engineering receive substantial attention, while the work behind books, papers, code, and other training material is often unpaid. The authors contend that compensation for this work should be the largest expense.

To ground that position, they study 64 language models released between 2016 and 2024. They estimate what it would cost to pay people to create each model’s training dataset from scratch. Even with highly conservative wage assumptions, the estimated dataset-production costs are 10 to 1,000 times the costs of training the models themselves.

The comparison puts a monetary scale on labor that ordinary training-cost accounts can overlook. It is a reconstruction-cost estimate, so its meaning depends on the stated exercise of paying for equivalent production from scratch. The authors use the resulting gap to argue that providers face a substantial financial liability and to motivate research directions toward fairer compensation practices.
icml-2025-position-the-most-expensive-pa.tldr: Estimated labor costs to recreate training datasets for 64 language models exceed model-training costs by 10 to 1,000 times.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that sustained self-improvement requires agents to evaluate and adapt their own learning processes. Current approaches often use rigid improvement procedures that transfer poorly between task domains and struggle as capabilities grow. The authors call the proposed internal capacity intrinsic metacognitive learning, drawing inspiration from how humans reflect on their own learning.

Their framework contains three components. Metacognitive knowledge covers an agent’s assessment of its capabilities, tasks, and learning strategies. Metacognitive planning determines what to learn and how to approach it. Metacognitive evaluation reflects on learning experiences so that future learning can improve. Together, these components describe control over the learning process itself.

Analyzing existing agents, the authors find that metacognitive control is mostly supplied through fixed, human-designed loops. They argue that many ingredients for more intrinsic control are already available, while identifying important remaining questions. These include distributing responsibilities between people and agents and evaluating the resulting learning reliably. The framework is intended to guide progress toward sustained, generalizable, aligned improvement rather than establish that such improvement has already been achieved.
icml-2025-position-truly-self-improving-.tldr: The authors argue that self-improving agents need internal capacities to assess, plan, and revise how they learn.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that uncertainty needs a richer treatment when language-model agents interact with people. Traditional approaches summarize ambiguity with one number or divide it into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. Reviewing the literature, the authors find conflicting definitions of those categories and argue that their meanings break down in open, interactive agent settings.

They propose three research directions. Underspecification uncertainty concerns information or task requirements that a user has not yet supplied. Interactive learning would let an agent reduce uncertainty about the situation by asking follow-up questions. Output uncertainty concerns expressing ambiguity through the possibilities of language and speech, beyond simply attaching a numerical confidence value.

The proposal treats uncertainty as part of an evolving conversation: the task can become clearer through interaction, and the way uncertainty is communicated can itself be richer. The authors expect these directions to make agent interactions more transparent, trustworthy, and intuitive. Those benefits are a research expectation, while the paper’s immediate contribution is its critique of existing categories and its interaction-focused agenda.
icml-2025-position-uncertainty-quantific.tldr: The paper proposes studying incomplete requests, clarifying interactions, and expressive uncertainty communication for language-model agents.

paragraphs: This position paper starts from the premise that humans and machines have different concepts. It frames interpretability as a communication problem: people need ways to refer to and control machine concepts, while machines need ways to receive precisely expressed human concepts. The authors argue that existing human vocabulary is insufficient for this shared task.

Their proposal is to develop neologisms, or new words, that can form a shared human–machine language. These terms should strike a useful balance in abstraction. A term that is too detailed may apply only in narrow circumstances, while one that is too broad may fail to communicate the precise concept needed for understanding or control.

The authors demonstrate two proofs of concept. A length neologism enables control over language-model response length, and a diversity neologism enables sampling more varied responses. These examples illustrate how newly introduced concepts can support specific forms of control. The broader claim is that expanding shared vocabulary could improve both understanding and interaction, with the demonstrations serving as initial evidence for that direction.
icml-2025-position-we-cant-understand-ai.tldr: New shared human–machine terms could improve AI understanding and control, illustrated through response-length and diversity concepts.

paragraphs: This position paper asks which algorithms language models actually use when solving problems. The authors argue that attention to performance through scale has left this question underexplored. They propose AlgEval, a framework for systematically investigating the computational building blocks models learn and how those pieces combine to solve particular tasks.

AlgEval directs investigation toward internal representations, attention, and computation performed during inference. A case study on emerging search algorithms illustrates two complementary approaches. Researchers first formulate hypotheses about candidate algorithms, then test those hypotheses through analysis of attention patterns and hidden states at the circuit level. This connects a proposed account of problem solving with evidence inside the model.

The intended contribution is a more understandable explanation of computation than performance scores alone provide. The authors argue that such knowledge could guide more sample-efficient training, better performance, and new architectures for individual and multi-agent systems. These are potential benefits of the research program; the case study illustrates how algorithmic investigation can proceed rather than establishing all of those downstream outcomes.
icml-2025-position-we-need-an-algorithmi.tldr: AlgEval proposes systematic investigation of the algorithms language models learn, combining algorithmic hypotheses with internal circuit analysis.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that meaningful scientific and societal progress with AI requires research grounded in the settings where systems will be used. The proposed approach, responsible application-driven AI, asks researchers to engage with ethical and legal considerations, practical constraints, and public discussion. The needs and values of affected communities are part of the research problem.

The authors organize the approach into three stages. First, researchers build teams spanning disciplines and conduct studies centered on people. Second, they develop methods, assumptions, ethical commitments, and evaluation measures suited to the specific context. Third, they test and sustain effectiveness using staged testbeds and an ongoing community of practice.

The stages connect problem selection, method design, and continued assessment. This matters because the paper’s vision of useful AI depends on technical feasibility and responsiveness to local circumstances together. The contribution is a proposed research process for pursuing that combination. The authors present it as a way to unlock value for communities, rather than reporting that one general method already meets every application’s needs.
icml-2025-position-we-need-responsible-a.tldr: RAD-AI proposes a three-stage research process connecting community needs, context-specific methods, and sustained evaluation.

paragraphs: This paper examines the gap between generating a virtual 3D object and producing a representation suitable for manufacturing. Many generative models emphasize rendered appearance without accounting for processes such as milling, casting, or injection molding. The authors argue that manufacturing requires information and structure that current representations often fail to provide.

They identify missing machine-readable manufacturing semantics, difficulty breaking complex shapes into parameterized parts suitable for computer-aided manufacturing, and inadequate scoring methods for comparing generated outputs with true reconstructions. They also demonstrate that existing generative models for computer-aided design fail to generalize beyond their training datasets or to unmodified objects created by humans.

To direct research toward these problems, the authors provide more realistic datasets and baseline benchmarks. Their evaluations find that existing models are severely overfit to simpler data. This connects the representation problem with an evaluation problem: success on simplified examples does not establish performance on the more realistic objects examined. The contribution supplies concrete evaluation resources alongside a call to make manufacturability central to research.
icml-2025-position-you-cant-manufacture-.tldr: More realistic datasets expose severe overfitting in existing generative CAD models and highlight the gap between visual 3D assets and manufacturable designs.
